AI grading set to reshape tobacco auctions in Andhra Pradesh

The Tobacco Board is preparing to test AI-based grading for FCV tobacco bales in Andhra Pradesh with Constems AI. The pilot aims to reduce subjectivity, speed up auctions and improve price discovery for farmers.
  • ETAgriculture
  • Published On Aug 11, 2026 at 03:48 PM IST
India’s tobacco auctions are set for a technology-led reset as the Tobacco Board moves to test artificial intelligence in grading one of the country’s most commercially sensitive farm products. The shift is aimed at reducing disputes over quality, speeding up auction decisions and bringing a more standardised approach to pricing at the mandi level.
From manual assessment to machine-assisted grading
According to The Hindu BusinessLine, the Administrator of the Tobacco Board, which functions under the Union Ministry of Commerce and Industry, has joined hands with Constems AI Private Ltd to introduce AI-based grading for Flue-Cured Virginia, or FCV, tobacco bales at select auction platforms in Andhra Pradesh. The arrangement is expected to make grading less dependent on individual judgement and more anchored in data-driven assessment.
At present, FCV tobacco grading is carried out manually by trained classifiers. The system has long relied on expertise built over years of field experience, but that same dependence on human judgement can also introduce variation from one assessment to another. For farmers, that variation matters because the grade assigned to a bale directly affects the price realised in the auction yard.
Why the board is turning to AI now
The move reflects a broader push in Indian agriculture to use digital tools where pricing depends heavily on visual inspection and subjective evaluation. In tobacco, where buyers and sellers often argue over quality parameters, a more uniform grading mechanism can help lower friction and improve confidence in the transaction process.
Constems AI co-founder and chief technology officer Amit Srivastava said the partnership will use computer vision and deep learning to make tobacco grading quicker, more consistent and more transparent. His comments, as reported by The Hindu BusinessLine, point to a central challenge in the sector: quality must be assessed rapidly, but the process must also be trusted by all sides involved in the sale.
Srivastava also noted that because the grade of a tobacco bale has a direct bearing on market value, a standardised and technology-supported framework has become increasingly important. That logic is particularly relevant in auction systems, where even small differences in perceived quality can alter farmer income and buyer bidding behaviour.
How the system is expected to work
Constems AI will deploy its CAInatics vision engine and 3N, described by the company as a large vision modal model, to analyse images of tobacco bales and assign grades. The output is then delivered instantly on the grader’s mobile application, allowing decisions to be made more quickly at the auction platform.
The immediate appeal of such a system lies in speed and consistency. In a high-volume environment, auction officials need a process that can handle large batches without slowing trade. For farmers, faster grading can mean shorter waiting times and a clearer understanding of how their produce is being valued. For buyers, a more traceable system can reduce uncertainty and help support repeatable procurement decisions.
Technology-led grading also has a governance angle. When the same visual inputs are assessed through a standard model, the scope for variation between different classifiers can be narrowed. That does not eliminate the need for human oversight, but it can create a more auditable baseline for price discovery in a sector where trust is central to the market structure.
What it could mean for growers and buyers
If the pilot performs as intended, the biggest beneficiaries are likely to be growers who have often depended on the judgement of individual classifiers. Objective grading can improve the odds of a fairer assessment, especially in cases where produce quality is close to the boundary between two grades. Better consistency may also reduce the number of disputes at auction centres, which can otherwise slow down sales and delay payment cycles.
For the broader tobacco supply chain, the experiment could become a reference point for other commodity markets that still rely heavily on visual inspection. Agricultural grading in India remains uneven across crops and regions, and the tobacco sector offers a useful test case because grading directly influences value and is conducted in a structured auction environment.
There is also a strategic dimension for the Tobacco Board itself. By introducing AI into grading, the board signals that digital tools can be used not just for record-keeping or market information, but for the core commercial act that determines price. If the model proves reliable across auction platforms, it could influence how other agri-commodities are assessed in future.
A wider signal for Indian agri-tech
The development comes at a time when Indian agriculture is seeing growing interest in AI applications that go beyond crop advisory and into trade, logistics and quality control. The tobacco grading initiative suggests that the next phase of agri-tech adoption may be less about farm inputs and more about the market infrastructure that sits between the field and the buyer.
That makes the Andhra Pradesh rollout significant even if the initial coverage is limited. A successful implementation could show that machine vision can function in a live auction setting, where speed, accuracy and acceptance all matter at once. It may also encourage regulators and commodity boards to consider similar tools for other products where visual grading still dominates.
For now, the focus is on proving that technology can reduce subjectivity without disrupting the auction process. If that balance is achieved, the use of AI in tobacco grading could become one of the more practical examples of digital transformation in Indian agriculture, where the financial impact is measured not in abstract efficiency gains but in the price a farmer receives for every bale sold.
